newsitem.title: UK: Asian vehicle glut threatens Europeans.
newsitem.headline: Asian vehicle glut threatens Europeans.

text.p: Massive overcapacity among Asian automobile makers will produce a chronic need for new markets and could threaten weaker European firms like Renault, Peugeot and Fiat, according to a report published on Tuesday.
And over-optimistic vehicle sales growth projections for the region are being slashed, according to the report.

The report, from the Economist Intelligence Unit, said by 2000 total capacity for cars, commercial vehicles and trucks in the Asia-Pacific region will be around 13.8 million a year, with sales locally expected to reach only 7.5 million.
This excess capacity is likely to be aimed at markets in north America and Europe, according to E.I.U. associate editor Graeme Maxton.

"Weaker competitors like (France's) Renault and Peugeot and Fiat of Italy are likely to suffer from an export drive from Asia. They are all based in high cost countries by world standards, in low growth markets and over-dependent on sales in their home countries," Maxton told Reuters.
Maxton saw less of a threat to north American markets because of the poorer quality of Asia-Pacific cars.

The E.I.U. report entitled "The emerging automotive markets of Asia--Pacific: The myth of major growth is exposed", said sales of cars would rise to 5.2 million in 2005 from about three million in 1996.
The Asia-Pacific region ranges from Pakistan in the west to Indonesia in the south and South Korea in the east.

"This is a compound annual growth rate of 6.4 per cent, three times the rate anticipated in the developed markets. However, this is lower than that expected by many in ther industry who predicted a market of 10 million units a year or more by 2005," the report said.
Maxton said key countries like China, South Korea and Taiwan all had lower growth than expected, hit by various maladies including inflation, and market saturation.
The study also found that there will be massive overcapacity in the region by 2000, almost double local demand although the rapid growth of the early 1990s had ended.
It said growth would continue, but at a slower rate although rapid growth in South Korea had ended and sales are now flat.
The report said South Korea will dominate production over the next decade, with annual car and truck production reaching 3.5 million in 2005, nearly a third of the regions's total.
"By 2000, three South Korean firms aim to be among the top ten in the world - Hyundai, Daewoo, Kia Motors Corp, while Samsung Co, the latest entrant plans to join them by 2010," the report said.
But Korea, and other countries, are storing up trouble for themselves.

"The Koreans are beginning to realise they've got this problem. They will have capacity of more than three million vehicles than they need for domestic demand in 2000. India will be able to make 1.2 million more than it can sell domestically," Maxton said.
